lines.text: M15 lesson 1 of 16 | Primary practice: practice/fabric_patterns/01_cloud_boundary.py
Why this matters
Cloud data engineering is not simply 'running the same laptop code on somebody else's computer.' The cloud
changes ownership boundaries, identity, billing, durability, network reachability and failure assumptions. A junior
engineer who can draw those boundaries is safer than one who memorizes service names. In Fabric, much of
the infrastructure is SaaS-managed, but you still own the data contract, access model, workload behavior and
evidence that a run produced the right result.
Picture it in your head
Picture three layers of responsibility. Microsoft operates the physical platform and much of the service fabric.
Your organization chooses capacity, tenant/workspace governance and identities. Your data team chooses
items, schemas, pipelines, code, validation and promotion. When an incident happens, ask first which boundary
owns the failed component instead of randomly changing settings.
New words before use

rows: The organization-level identity and administration boundary.
A pool of Fabric compute resources measured in Capacity Units (CUs).
A collaboration/security container that holds Fabric items.
A Fabric object such as a lakehouse, notebook, pipeline or warehouse.
The path where actual data is read, written or processed.

Follow with me once
A regional courier company wants one platform for parcel scan files, transformations and analytics. The beginner
answer is 'put everything in Fabric.' The engineering answer decomposes it: a workspace contains the
lakehouse, notebooks and pipeline; OneLake holds durable data; Fabric compute executes Spark/SQL/pipeline
work; Entra identities decide who may operate the workspace; capacity determines how much shared compute
is available. The source system remains an external dependency. If the source API is down, adding more Fabric
capacity does not repair the source. If a notebook lacks permission, restarting Spark does not grant
authorization.
Write those components in a table with columns: component, owner, durable state, identity used, observable
evidence, recovery action. This is a simple exercise, but it is the beginning of production reasoning.
What you should see
You can point at every box in a small cloud data-flow diagram and say what it stores, what executes there, who
authorizes it, what it costs broadly, and what proof would show that it worked.
Why it worked
The design separates service names from responsibilities. That lets you reason when the product UI changes
because storage, compute, identity, orchestration and observation are still distinct concerns.
Break it / common failure
A common mistake is assuming SaaS means 'nothing to operate.' Fabric removes server patching and cluster
provisioning work, but your team still owns bad joins, duplicate loads, over-broad access, runaway scans,
broken dependencies and untested deployments. Another mistake is thinking a green pipeline run proves
business correctness.
Reason through a realistic incident
A notebook is slow and the capacity dashboard shows throttling. At the same time, a source API is returning 429
responses. Do not collapse these into one vague 'cloud is slow' incident. Separate source throttling from Fabric
capacity pressure, record which stage waits, and test one hypothesis at a time.
Deepen the engineering reasoning
Cloud architecture becomes easier when you name state. Configuration state lives in workspace/item
definitions; durable business data lives in OneLake or external systems; transient compute state lives in running
jobs; deployment state lives in Git/pipeline metadata; progress state might live in a watermark table. Recovery
depends on restoring the correct state, not simply rerunning everything. Also distinguish scalability from
elasticity: a service may scale to large workloads, while elasticity describes adjusting resources to demand.
Finally, recognize cost as a correctness-adjacent constraint: a pipeline that produces the right table by scanning
50 TB every five minutes can still be an unacceptable production design.
Now you do a changed version alone
Draw a six-box architecture for orders arriving from an operational database into a Fabric lakehouse and then a
gold table. Label storage, compute, identity and monitoring boundaries. Do not use more than two Fabric
compute item types.
Fresh changed retry
Change the source from an Azure database to an on-premises database behind a firewall. Add only the new
connectivity/gateway/private-access concern; keep the rest of the architecture stable.

Keep the genuine first failure. A repaired run is repair evidence; the changed retry is mastery evidence.
Ready-made revision
Cloud DE = managed platform plus your explicit responsibilities for data, identity, orchestration, evidence and
cost. Diagnose by boundary, not by brand name.

M15 lesson 2 of 16 | Primary practice: practice/fabric_patterns/02_rbac_scope_simulator.py
Why this matters
Most serious cloud data incidents are easier to create with permissions than with Python. Identity and access
management (IAM) determines who or what can create resources, read data, run pipelines and retrieve secrets.
Least privilege is not a slogan: it is the discipline of granting the smallest practical permission at the smallest
practical scope for the shortest practical time.
Picture it in your head
Picture a keyring. Identity answers 'whose keyring is this?' Authentication proves that identity. Authorization
checks whether a specific key opens a specific door. Azure RBAC adds three pieces to every permission
decision: principal, role and scope. Fabric workspace roles add another collaboration layer inside Fabric.
New words before use

rows: A user, group, service principal or managed identity requesting access.
A named set of allowed actions.
The resource boundary where a role assignment applies.
Deciding what that identity may do.
Granting only the access required for the job.

Follow with me once
Suppose Priya develops a notebook that reads a bronze lakehouse and writes silver tables. She needs edit/run
access in the development workspace, but an analyst who consumes gold output may only need Viewer/read
permissions. A deployment service principal may need permission to update supported Fabric items without
needing interactive human access.
In the supplied simulator, create three assignments: Analyst -> Viewer at workspace DEV; Engineer ->
Contributor at workspace DEV; DeploymentSP -> Contributor at workspace TEST. Then ask whether Analyst
can delete a notebook, whether Engineer can edit it, and whether DeploymentSP can modify TEST. The result
should follow from principal + role + scope, not from the person's job title.
What you should see
You can explain why 'Contributor everywhere' is dangerous, distinguish workspace roles from Azure resource
roles, and reason about effective permissions without guessing.
Why it worked
Permissions become reviewable when each assignment has a concrete principal, role and scope. Least privilege
is impossible to verify when access is granted through vague shared accounts or undocumented owner-level
permissions.
Break it / common failure
Two beginner failures recur. First, giving a human account broad Owner/Admin access because a lab is blocked.
Second, confusing Microsoft Entra directory roles, Azure RBAC roles and Fabric workspace roles. They interact
with different resource planes. Fix the missing permission at the layer that actually denies the action.
Reason through a realistic incident
A pipeline worked yesterday under your personal account but fails when scheduled under a service identity. That
is valuable evidence: the code path is probably valid, while the runtime identity lacks some required permission
or connection. Compare effective identities and scopes before editing transformation logic.
Deepen the engineering reasoning
Machine identities deserve the same rigor as users. Prefer managed identities or federated/service identities
over embedding long-lived secrets when the platform supports them. Separate human development permissions
from production execution identity. Use groups where possible so access follows job function instead of dozens
of one-off grants. Remember that RBAC is usually additive: multiple assignments can combine into broader
effective access. The review question is not only 'can this identity run?' but also 'what else could this identity do if
compromised?'

Design roles for four personas: developer, data consumer, deployment automation and production support.
State the minimum workspace-level role and one thing each persona must not be allowed to do.

contractor cannot edit notebooks, pipelines or security configuration.

M15 lesson 3 of 16 | Primary practice: practice/fabric_patterns/03_storage_onelake_paths.py
Why this matters
Before Fabric, Azure data engineers often assembled storage accounts, ADLS Gen2 containers, compute
services and orchestration separately. OneLake keeps familiar data-lake ideas but presents one logical lake for
the Fabric tenant. You still need to understand files, folders, table areas, URIs and external storage because
shortcuts and interoperability depend on those boundaries.
Picture it in your head
Think of ADLS Gen2 as a set of storage accounts and containers you explicitly provision. Think of OneLake as
Fabric's tenant-wide logical lake where each Fabric item provisions its own storage view. A lakehouse gives you
a Files area for arbitrary files and a Tables area for managed/queryable table data.
New words before use

rows: Durable storage addressed by container/path rather than disk blocks.
Azure Data Lake Storage capabilities built on Blob Storage with hierarchical namespace.
Lakehouse location for arbitrary raw/semi-structured files.
Lakehouse location intended for managed table data, normally Delta.
Azure Blob FileSystem-style path that Spark-compatible engines can use.

Follow with me once
Create a path inventory for a lakehouse named ops_lh in workspace de_dev. Raw CSV lands under
Files/bronze/orders/2026/09/14/. A curated Delta table is exposed under Tables/silver_orders. Write the
human-readable logical path and the ABFS-style shape. Do not invent a local C: drive path; OneLake is remote
service storage.
The practice script validates that a path has a workspace, item name/type and Files/Tables boundary. It does
not pretend to authenticate to OneLake. That separation is intentional: path reasoning can be tested locally;
actual Entra-authenticated access remains learner-PC/Fabric proof.
abfss://<workspace>@onelake.dfs.fabric.microsoft.com/<lakehouse>.lakehouse/Files/bronze/orders/
What you should see
You can decide whether a dataset belongs in Files or Tables, read a OneLake path without panic, and explain
how OneLake differs from but interoperates with Azure storage concepts.
Why it worked
Storage design became explicit: raw file landing and managed tables are separate contracts even though both
live in OneLake. The path itself records enough context to avoid mysterious hard-coded mounts.
Break it / common failure
Do not assume anything placed under Files automatically appears as a SQL-queryable table. Conversely, do not
treat the Tables area as a dumping ground for random CSVs. Another mistake is hard-coding workspace/item
display names into production code without a configuration strategy for DEV/TEST/PROD.
Reason through a realistic incident
A notebook can read a file path but the SQL analytics endpoint cannot see it as a table. That is not automatically
a permission bug. Check whether the data is actually represented as a supported Delta table in the lakehouse
Tables area or exposed through an appropriate shortcut.
Deepen the engineering reasoning
Cloud storage paths are interfaces. Renaming a workspace or item, moving from DEV to PROD, or changing an
external source can break brittle strings. Prefer parameterized logical references, environment configuration and
documented ownership. Also distinguish physical copy from logical reference: OneLake shortcuts can expose
data without duplicating it, which changes freshness, security and failure reasoning. Finally, understand that
storage durability does not replace data-quality controls; a perfectly durable bad file is still bad data.

table. State why each location is chosen.

M15 lesson 4 of 16 | Primary practice: practice/fabric_patterns/04_workspace_inventory.json
Why this matters
Fabric feels simple because many workloads share one portal, but that simplicity can hide lifecycle boundaries.
A workspace is not just a folder. It is a collaboration, security, capacity and deployment boundary that contains
items such as lakehouses, notebooks, pipelines, warehouses and environments.
Picture it in your head
Imagine a workshop. The workspace is the locked room. Items are the machines and workbenches inside it.
Capacity is the shared electricity supply. People receive room-level roles, while some items may also have finer
permissions. Moving a machine to another room changes which room policies and collaborators surround it.
New words before use

rows: Container for Fabric items, collaboration and many security/lifecycle settings.
A first-class Fabric artifact such as Lakehouse, Notebook or Data pipeline.
Admin, Member, Contributor or Viewer access boundary.
Which Fabric capacity supplies compute for the workspace.
A Fabric item for Spark runtime/libraries/compute configuration.
A reference from one item to another, such as notebook -> lakehouse.

Then compare two architectures: one giant workspace containing DEV/TEST/PROD suffixes versus separate

You can inspect a Fabric workspace and explain what each item does, what it depends on and why workspace

An item inventory turns the portal from a collection of icons into a dependency graph. That makes missing

convenient. Another is assuming a workspace role automatically grants every data-plane permission in every
connected external system.

A notebook deploys successfully to TEST but opens with a broken default lakehouse reference. The notebook

bindings instead of rerunning the same deployment.

Workspace design influences blast radius. Admin rights on a small DEV workspace are very different from

metadata so a new engineer can understand the topology without tribal knowledge. Keep environment-specific

a notebook, its environment, target lakehouse and required connection should be reviewed together.

M15 lesson 5 of 16 | Primary practice: practice/fabric_patterns/05_shortcut_decision.py
Why this matters
Shortcuts are one of Fabric's most important 'do not copy unless you must' features. They let OneLake expose
data that physically lives elsewhere or in another Fabric item. This can reduce duplicate storage and simplify
access, but it also means freshness, authorization and availability depend on the referenced source.
Picture it in your head
A shortcut is like a sign in one warehouse aisle that says 'the boxes are actually stored in Building B; follow this
address.' The local directory looks convenient, but there is no second independent copy. If Building B denies
access or goes down, the sign cannot manufacture the boxes.
New words before use

rows: A OneLake reference to data stored at another supported location.
A physically duplicated dataset under your control.
The authoritative dataset whose changes drive downstream data.
Access whose success depends on identity/permissions at another boundary.
How far a viewed dataset lags the authoritative source.
Storage outside the current Fabric item/workspace.

Use rule: Videos are strongly encouraged because this course is designed for visual learning. Current official

flow and then reconcile commands/capabilities with the current docs.
Follow with me once
A sales team already has curated Delta data in a central lakehouse. Finance wants to query the same data.
Option A copies 200 GB nightly into a finance lakehouse. Option B creates a OneLake shortcut to the curated
table/folder. If Finance only needs read access and the source ownership/SLA are acceptable, the shortcut may
avoid duplication and preserve one source of truth. If Finance needs an independently frozen month-end
snapshot, a shortcut alone may not satisfy the requirement.
Run the shortcut decision script with fields copy_required, independent_retention, source_sla_acceptable and
source_format_delta. The output is a recommendation plus reasons, not a magical product rule.
What you should see
You can explain when a shortcut is elegant and when a physical copy is justified, including the security and
availability trade-off.
Why it worked
The decision starts from business guarantees - independent retention, freshness, ownership - rather than
choosing shortcuts just because they are new.
Break it / common failure
Do not promise independent disaster recovery from a shortcut to the same upstream data. Do not assume a
shortcut changes the underlying file format into Delta. And do not forget that consumers still need permissions
appropriate to the path through which they access the data.
Reason through a realistic incident
A table exposed through a shortcut suddenly fails for one team while the source owner can still read it. Compare
the consuming identity, shortcut configuration, source permissions and source health. Copying the data
immediately may hide the real authorization problem and create uncontrolled duplicates.
Deepen the engineering reasoning
A shortcut is a data-contract decision. Document source owner, expected freshness, schema-change process,
retention and support contact. When you build medallion layers across domains, shortcuts can provide governed
access to existing data products without centralizing every byte. But that decoupling works only if ownership is
explicit. Also consider performance: remote/reference access patterns can behave differently from local
managed tables, so measure important queries rather than promising zero-copy is always faster.

dimension - choose shortcut or copy and defend the decision.

source workspace is unavailable. Revisit your decision.

Keep Fabric and Databricks terms separate

OneLake and its shortcuts are part of the Fabric route taught here. Unity Catalog is Databricks governance; DBFS mount examples belong to a Databricks environment. Do not copy a mount-based tutorial into a Fabric notebook and assume the storage or permission model is the same. An integration between platforms must name both sides and its access boundary. Different doors, same underlying lakehouse table state.

schema, and writes a Delta table Tables/silver_orders. A gold table aggregates daily sales. Spark owns the
transformation/write path. The SQL analytics endpoint exposes the Delta tables for read-oriented T-SQL

What you should see
You can say exactly which engine writes the table, which surface queries it, and where the durable data lives.
You do not call every Fabric SQL surface a warehouse.
Why it worked
The design preserves one durable table contract while allowing multiple query/processing experiences. That
reduces unnecessary data copies and keeps reconciliation centered on one Delta state.
Break it / common failure
A frequent mistake is trying to INSERT/UPDATE lakehouse Delta tables through the SQL analytics endpoint as
if it were a normal writable SQL database. Another is assuming an arbitrary external Delta location will
automatically appear in the endpoint without supported registration/shortcut behavior.

metadata/synchronization state, and compare counts by a stable boundary. Do not rewrite data merely to force
visibility unless the root cause is understood.

The lakehouse is a convergence point, not an excuse to abandon modeling discipline. Delta ACID protects table
transactions, but it does not choose the correct grain or business key. Schema evolution is a tool, not permission
to accept uncontrolled drift. Maintain raw evidence, explicit transformation stages and reconciliation. Also note
the runtime distinction: M13's local/reference Spark 4.2 + Delta 4.4 baseline is not the same thing as Fabric's
service-managed runtime. In Fabric Runtime 2.0, the current GA combination is Spark 4.1 + Delta 4.2; write
code against the actual service runtime you are using.

which are queried from the SQL endpoint.

M15 lesson 7 of 16 | Primary practice: practice/fabric_patterns/07_notebook_patterns.py
Why this matters
A notebook is useful because code, explanation and results can sit together. That convenience becomes
dangerous when a production pipeline depends on a 600-cell document with hidden state and manual clicks.
Good Fabric notebooks behave like reviewable programs: explicit inputs, small functions, parameters,
deterministic outputs, validation and a clear execution path.
Picture it in your head
Treat a notebook as a thin orchestration shell around reusable logic, not as a scratchpad that accidentally
became production. Markdown explains the contract; parameter cells define inputs; functions/modules hold
repeated logic; validation cells prove outputs; the final cell returns a clear status/value.
New words before use

rows: Variables/results created by prior cell execution.
Supplying environment/run values instead of hard-coding them.

**Target proof:** after initial + changes runs, `silver_orders` has **5 unique orders** and the paid revenue is **460.00**. Do not mark LIVE FABRIC PASS unless you actually obtain the portal/run/table evidence in your own tenant.
0. Access and cost guardrail

Preferred learning route: use an eligible Microsoft Fabric trial or an existing Fabric-enabled workspace. Microsoft currently documents a 60-day trial, but eligibility depends on tenant/region/settings and can change.

If you cannot start a trial, **do not buy capacity just to satisfy this course**. Complete the local `fabric_patterns/16_end_to_end_local_case.py` control, study this walkthrough, and record `LIVE FABRIC = PENDING - ACCESS UNAVAILABLE`. Return to the real build when you have legitimate trial/workspace access.
Official references:
- Trial: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/fabric/get-started/fabric-trial
- Lakehouse tutorial: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/fabric/data-engineering/tutorial-lakehouse-get-started/
- OneLake/lakehouse upload: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/fabric/onelake/create-lakehouse-onelake
- Notebook activity: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-ca/fabric/data-factory/notebook-activity
- Pipeline parameters: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/fabric/data-factory/parameters
1. Create the DEV workspace and lakehouse

2. Create a workspace named `de2026-m15-dev` (add your initials if the name must be unique).
3. Assign the workspace to your eligible trial/paid Fabric capacity.
4. In the workspace select **New item -> Lakehouse**.
5. Name it `orders_lh`.
6. Open the lakehouse. Confirm you can see both **Files** and **Tables**.
Evidence: save the workspace name and lakehouse name. Do not screenshot secrets or tenant IDs unnecessarily.
2. Upload the supplied course files into OneLake
From the extracted course package use:
- `14_M15/practice/data/orders_initial.csv`
- `14_M15/practice/data/orders_changes.csv`
In the lakehouse Files area create `m15/orders/` and upload both files so the notebook paths are:

3. Create notebook `nb_m15_orders`
Create a notebook in the same workspace, attach `orders_lh` as the default lakehouse, and add the following cells in order.
Use the complete companion file `FABRIC_GUIDED_BUILD_NOTEBOOK.py`. It is divided into five cells. Copy each cell below in order. Mark only Cell 1 as the parameter cell.
Cell 1 - PARAMETERS: mark THIS cell as the Fabric parameter cell.
p_batch = "initial"
p_expected_rows = 3
p_expected_paid_revenue = "200.50"
p_fail_after_silver = False
Cell 2 - READ AND VALIDATE; no table changes here.
from decimal import Decimal
from pyspark.sql import functions as F, types as T, Window
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.session.timeZone", "UTC")
if p_batch not in {"initial", "changes", "conflict", "newer", "interrupt"}:
raise ValueError("unsupported batch; use one supplied course file")
fields = ["order_id", "updated_at", "customer_id", "amount", "status"]
schema = T.StructType([T.StructField(x, T.StringType()) for x in fields])
raw = (spark.read.option("header", True).option("enforceSchema", False)
.schema(schema).csv(f"Files/m15/orders/orders_{p_batch}.csv"))
if raw.limit(1).count() == 0:
raise ValueError("empty batch: inspect the file before advancing progress")
staged = (raw.withColumn("event_ts", F.try_to_timestamp("updated_at"))
.withColumn("amount_dec", F.expr("try_cast(amount AS DECIMAL(12,2))")))
invalid = F.lit(False)
for name in fields:
invalid = invalid | F.col(name).isNull() | (F.length(F.trim(F.col(name))) == 0)
invalid = (invalid | F.col("event_ts").isNull()
| F.col("amount_dec").isNull()
| ~F.col("status").isin("NEW", "PAID", "CANCELLED"))
bad = staged.filter(invalid)
if bad.limit(1).count():
bad.show(truncate=False)
raise ValueError("invalid input: no business table or checkpoint was changed")
incoming_all = staged.select("order_id", "customer_id",
F.col("amount_dec").alias("amount"), "status", "event_ts").dropDuplicates()
# Same key/version with different content is ambiguous, even if order differs.
conflicts = incoming_all.groupBy("order_id", "event_ts").count().filter("count > 1")
if conflicts.limit(1).count():
conflicts.show(truncate=False)
raise ValueError("equal-version conflict inside the input")
w = Window.partitionBy("order_id").orderBy(F.col("event_ts").desc())
incoming = incoming_all.withColumn("rn", F.row_number().over(w)).filter("rn = 1").drop("rn")
Cell 3 - COMPARE WITH EXISTING STATE; initial is NOT an overwrite command.
exists = spark.catalog.tableExists("silver_orders")
if not exists and p_batch != "initial":
raise ValueError("bootstrap once with initial before applying changes")
current = spark.table("silver_orders") if exists else incoming.limit(0)
if current.groupBy("order_id").count().filter("count > 1").limit(1).count():
raise ValueError("target key conflict: inspect Silver before writing")
s, t = incoming.alias("s"), current.alias("t")
paired = s.join(t, F.col("s.order_id") == F.col("t.order_id"), "inner")
changed = F.lit(False)
for name in ("customer_id", "amount", "status"):
changed = changed | ~F.col("s." + name).eqNullSafe(F.col("t." + name))
if paired.filter((F.col("s.event_ts") == F.col("t.event_ts")) & changed).limit(1).count():
raise ValueError("equal-version conflict against Silver; no write allowed")
updates = (s.join(t, F.col("s.order_id") == F.col("t.order_id"), "left")
.filter(F.col("t.order_id").isNull() | (F.col("s.event_ts") > F.col("t.event_ts")))
.select("s.*"))
projected = current.join(updates.select("order_id"), "order_id", "left_anti").unionByName(updates)
Cell 4 - CHECK THE PROPOSED RESULT BEFORE WRITING.
row_count = projected.count()
paid = projected.filter("status = 'PAID'").agg(F.sum("amount")).first()[0]
paid = Decimal(str(paid or 0)).quantize(Decimal("0.01"))
expected = Decimal(str(p_expected_paid_revenue))
if not expected.is_finite() or row_count != int(p_expected_rows) or paid != expected:
raise ValueError(f"reconciliation failed BEFORE write: rows={row_count}, paid={paid}")
# A checkpoint is a high-water mark over processed versions, not a wall-clock time.
row_max = incoming.agg(F.max("event_ts")).first()[0]
control_exists = spark.catalog.tableExists("m15_pipeline_control")
if control_exists:
ctl = spark.table("m15_pipeline_control")
if set(ctl.columns) != {"pipeline", "committed_ts"}:
raise ValueError("old control schema: use a fresh disposable M15 lakehouse")
previous = ctl.filter("pipeline = 'orders'").agg(F.max("committed_ts")).first()[0]
else:
previous = None
candidate = max(x for x in (previous, row_max) if x is not None)
print({"before": str(previous), "candidate": str(candidate), "rows": row_count, "paid": str(paid)})
Cell 5 - DURABLE SILVER, GOLD, THEN PROGRESS. Single-writer lab.
incoming.createOrReplaceTempView("m15_incoming")
if not exists:
# errorifexists prevents a concurrent/bootstrap rerun from replacing a table.
incoming.write.format("delta").mode("errorifexists").saveAsTable("silver_orders")
else:
spark.sql("""
MERGE INTO silver_orders t USING m15_incoming s
ON t.order_id = s.order_id
WHEN MATCHED AND s.event_ts > t.event_ts THEN UPDATE SET *
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *
if str(p_fail_after_silver).lower() == "true":
raise RuntimeError("DELIBERATE_FAILURE_AFTER_SILVER: Gold and progress remain unchanged")
# Reconcile actual durable Silver; another writer is not permitted in this lab.
silver = spark.table("silver_orders")
actual_paid = silver.filter("status = 'PAID'").agg(F.sum("amount")).first()[0] or Decimal("0")
if silver.count() != row_count or actual_paid != paid:
raise ValueError("durable Silver differs: stop before Gold/progress")
gold = spark.createDataFrame([(row_count, paid)], "unique_orders long, paid_revenue decimal(18,2)")
gold.write.format("delta").mode("overwrite").saveAsTable("gold_order_summary")
new_control = spark.createDataFrame([("orders", candidate)], "pipeline string, committed_ts timestamp")
if not control_exists:
new_control.write.format("delta").mode("errorifexists").saveAsTable("m15_pipeline_control")
else:
new_control.createOrReplaceTempView("m15_next_control")
spark.sql("""
MERGE INTO m15_pipeline_control t USING m15_next_control s
ON t.pipeline = s.pipeline
WHEN MATCHED AND s.committed_ts > t.committed_ts THEN UPDATE SET *
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *
